links.why: Look at the tiger, the parrot and the crocodile: which ones have fur, feathers or scales, and how does each keep warm?
See how the camel, the polar bear's cousin and the monkey each have a body that suits where they live.
The deer eats grass and the tiger eats the deer, so this is a food chain you can see.
Let's count how many of each animal we saw and make a tally chart.
Tell me three words that describe your favourite animal.
The eight planets go around the Sun, and Earth is the third one from it.
People have seen patterns in the stars for thousands of years, and the nakshatras are one of them.
The Moon only looks like it changes shape because we see a different part of its lit side each night.
Day and night happen because Earth spins once around, so our side turns to face the Sun and then away.
Long ago people used the sky to make calendars and know when to sow seeds.
Every exhibit starts with a question, so what question could you ask about the one you liked best?
That lever or pulley lets a small push lift a big load.
The mirror maze works because light bounces off each mirror and comes to your eyes.
If we want to test it, we change one thing and keep everything else the same.
Explain to me one thing you learned there as if I had never been.

acts.name: Museum visit
words: saw old things in a museum

links.why: These old things show us how people lived long before we were born.
Look at the pot, the coin and the cloth: which material is each made from, and where does it come from?
Which new word did you learn on the labels today?
Write two sentences about the object you liked best.
Objects from different states show how people in each part of India live and speak.
Kings built this fort a long time ago to keep their people safe.
Thick stone walls keep a building standing for hundreds of years and keep the inside cool.
People used ramps, pulleys and levers to lift heavy stones this high.
Look for arches, domes and circles in the walls and towers.
Let's pace out the wall and see how many steps long it is.
Temples are places where families come together for prayer and festivals.
Look at the carvings and the gopuram: both sides match, which is called symmetry.
Flowers, lamps and sweets for a festival all come from people's work and the seasons.
The shiny brass lamp bounces light back at us, which is why it gleams.
मंदिर में जो देखा, उसे हिंदी में बताओ। (Tell me in Hindi what you saw in the temple.)
A mosque is where people come together to pray, and Eid is a happy festival they share.
The arches and the domes match on both sides, which is symmetry.
Look at the tiles and the carvings: the same design repeats again and again.
The call to prayer carries far because the sound waves travel through the air to us.
People of the neighbourhood meet here and help each other.
Christmas and Easter are festivals families celebrate together at church and at home.
Sunlight passes through coloured glass and splits the room into colour.
The church bell rings and its sound spreads out through the air as waves.
Look for arches, circles and triangles in the roof and the windows.
A hymn is a song with words that rhyme and a tune that repeats.
In the langar everyone sits together and shares the same meal, and volunteers help cook and serve.
If 200 people come and each gets 2 rotis, how many rotis must be made?
The dal, the wheat and the vegetables all began in a field and were grown by farmers.
Baisakhi and Gurpurab are festivals many families celebrate together.
पंजाबी और हिंदी के कौन से शब्द आज सुने? (Which Punjabi and Hindi words did you hear today?)
If the tomatoes cost 40 rupees and you pay 50, how much change should you get back?
The shopkeeper uses a weighing scale to find how heavy the vegetables are.
The farmer sells to a trader, the trader sells to the shopkeeper, and then we buy it.
This brinjal grew on a plant and travelled to this stall.
What are the names of the vegetables and fruits in English and in our own language?
Trains carry thousands of people and goods across the country every day.
The board says the train comes at 6:45, so how many minutes until then?
The map on the wall shows which way the train goes and which stations come next.
Look at all the ways people arrive: bus, auto, taxi and on foot.
The brakes press on the wheels, and friction stops the heavy train.
The wings push air down, and the air pushes the plane up.
Pilots listen to the wind and the weather because air carries the plane.
The plane leaves at 2:30 and lands at 4:10, so how long is the flight?
The route on the screen shows the way the plane flies from one city to another.
The air gets thinner as you go up, which is why rockets must carry their own air.
Outside the window, the land, houses, food and language change as the train goes across states.
The train started at 9 at night and arrives at 7 in the morning, so how many hours is the journey?
Let's follow the stations on the map with your finger.
When the train starts you lean back, because your body wants to stay where it was.
Write a short story about who you met on the train.
Roads, buses and trucks move people and goods from place to place.
The milestone says 120 km, so how far is it still to go?
Which way are we going: north, south, east or west?
Seat belts and traffic lights keep everyone safe on the road.
Tyres have a pattern of grooves so they grip the road, even in rain.
The wave moves in towards the shore, but the water itself mostly goes up and down.
Crabs, shells and seaweed live where the sea meets the land.
Sea water tastes salty because salt has dissolved in it.
Salt pans use the Sun to dry up sea water and leave the salt behind.
Sand is tiny pieces of broken rock and shell.
The river's water came from rain and snow far up in the hills, and flows to the sea.
Fish, frogs and plants all live in or beside the river.
Towns use river water for drinking, farms and washing, so it must be kept clean.
When people throw rubbish or waste into the river, the water and the animals suffer.
Many cities in India grew up beside rivers, because people need water.
It is colder on the hill, so let's read the thermometer at the bottom and at the top.
Plants and animals on the mountain have thick coats and small leaves to handle the cold.
Clouds rise up the hill, cool down and turn into rain or snow.
How many steps do you think it is to the top?
Mountains, plains and rivers are all kinds of land you can find on a map of India.
The wheat in our roti grew in a field like this one.
Soil is made from broken rock and dead plants, and worms mix it for the crops.
A seed needs water and warmth to sprout.
Plants need sun, water and air, and the farmer makes sure they get them.
The farmer works all year, so let's ask what the work is in each season.
In a village many families know each other and help one another.
Cows, goats, hens and dogs live close to people in a village.
Where does the village get its water from: a well, a hand pump or a tap?
A potter, a farmer and a weaver each do a job the village needs.
गाँव के लोग कौन से शब्द बोलते हैं? (Which words did the village people use?)
A letter travels by hand, van, train and plane before it reaches its home.
A letter has the date, the person's name, your message and your name.
अपने दोस्त को हिंदी में चिट्ठी लिखो। (Write a letter to a friend in Hindi.)
A stamp costs some rupees, so how much for three letters?
The postman and the sorting clerk do a job that keeps people in touch.
If you save 20 rupees every week, how much will you have after 5 weeks?
The passbook shows money put in and money taken out, so what is left?
A bank keeps people's money safe and lends some to others.
Never tell anyone your PIN or password, because it keeps your money safe.
If a toy costs 150 and you have 90, how many weeks of saving do you need?
A vaccine teaches your body how to fight a germ before the real one comes.
The doctor looks at your eyes, ears and throat to check each part is working well.
Doctors and nurses wash their hands often so germs do not spread.
The doctor measured how tall you are and how much you weigh, so how much have you grown?
Doctors, nurses and chemists are helpers who care for our health.
A library lets you borrow many stories and bring them home to read.
Pick a book and find three new words in it.
The book is due back in two weeks, so which date is that?
In the library we speak softly and look after the books so others can read them.
आज कौन सी हिंदी कहानी पढ़ी? (Which Hindi story did you read today?)
A longer swing takes more time to go back and forth than a shorter one.
You push the swing to start it, and gravity pulls it back.
Let's find a tree, a bush and a grass plant and see how they are different.
Sort what you saw in the park into plants, birds and insects.
The bees visit the flowers and the flowers feed the bees.
Raw things like milk, cotton or iron are turned into things we use.
Machines in a factory use wheels, levers and gears to do heavy work.
The machines need energy, such as electricity, to run.
Many people work together, and each does one part of the job.
Factories can make smoke and waste, so careful ones clean it before it goes out.
A mela is a happy gathering with food, games and craft that brings a whole area together.
You have 100 rupees: if the ride is 30 and a snack is 25, how much is left?
The giant wheel and the merry-go-round turn on an axle.
When the ride spins, you feel pushed outward, because things want to move in a straight line.
Folk dance, crafts and food at the mela show the culture of the place.
Diwali is the festival of lights, and families clean, decorate and share sweets.
Rangoli patterns are the same on both sides of a line, which is symmetry.
A diya burns because the flame has oil, air and heat.
How much will five diyas cost if each is 6 rupees?
Crackers make smoke and loud noise, which is why many families choose lights instead.
A wedding brings relatives from many places together, and each has a name for how they are related to us.
Let's draw the family tree and find who is whose uncle, aunt or cousin.
Each region has its own wedding songs, clothes and food.
If 150 guests sit at tables of 10, how many tables are needed?
The band is so loud that we should keep our ears safe by standing back.
Fish live in water and take the air dissolved in it.
Fish breathe with gills and find food by smell and sight.
The fish looks bigger or in a different place because light bends in water.
Sort the fish by colour, size or shape, and see which ways of sorting work best.
Count the fish of each kind and draw a bar chart.
Notice the birds' nests, food and calls: they show how each one lives.
Birds are the animals with feathers and wings, and they lay eggs.
The kingfisher eats fish and the fish eat small water creatures.
Sanctuaries keep forests and wetlands safe, so animals have a home.
Make a tally of how many of each bird you saw.
Compare a tree, a creeper and a herb and see how their stems differ.
Roots hold, stems carry, leaves make food, and flowers make seeds.
The seed grows into a plant and makes new seeds.
Leaves use light, air and water to make food for the plant.
Describe a leaf you found: its colour, shape and feel.
People made these long ago, and their stone, paint and carvings tell us how they lived.
Stone is hard and lasts a long time, while wood and cloth rot away.
Look for the pattern and the matching halves in the carvings.
Writing on the walls may be in an old script no longer used today.
How do people know how old this is? Let's ask what proof they have.
A dam holds water in a lake so that towns and fields can use it all year.
Bridges are made of triangles and arches, because those shapes stay strong.
The water pushes on the dam wall, so the wall is thicker at the bottom.
Canals carry water from the dam to the farms far away.
Count the triangles in the bridge.
Petrol stores energy that the engine uses to move the vehicle.
The pump measures litres, so how many litres fill a 10-litre tank?
If petrol costs 100 rupees a litre, how much for 3 litres?
Burning petrol makes smoke, so walking or cycling keeps the air cleaner.
A tyre needs grooves to grip the road.
Add up the prices of three things in the basket and find the total.
Guess how much the basket will cost, then check against the bill.
Read the label: which foods give us energy and which help us grow?
Check the date on the packet, because old food can make us sick.
A cloth bag can be used again and again, but a plastic bag is thrown away.
Firefighters and police help the whole neighbourhood stay safe.
Fire needs fuel, air and heat, and taking one away puts it out.
Know the emergency numbers and remember to call a grown-up first.
Each helper has special clothes and tools for the job.
Firefighters wear thick suits so heat does not reach their bodies.
Write about the trip: what you saw, who went and what you liked most.
The bus left at 8 and came back at 4, so how long was the trip?
Where did we go? Let's find the place on a map.
You felt tired from walking, because your muscles used up energy and need rest.
Tell the class about the trip in five sentences.
The oar pushes the water back, and the water pushes the boat forward.
Boats are made of wood, fibre or metal, which can float when shaped well.
Look out for birds, fish and plants that live in the lake or river.
In many places a boat or a ferry is how people cross the water.
Boats, trains and buses are all ways people travel.
Find the pole star and the Saptarishi, which people have used to find the way.
Look at the Moon tonight: is it getting bigger or smaller?
Stars are far-away suns, and the Moon only shines by reflecting sunlight.
Star light takes a very long time to reach us, so we see stars as they were long ago.
Which direction is the Moon in, and which way is north?
Processions are how communities show a festival and share it with everyone.
Festival foods and colours often come from plants and the season.
About how many people do you think are in the crowd?
Big chariots have large wheels and many people pulling, because friction makes them hard to move.
Drums and horns are loud, so keep a little way back to protect our ears.
Clay from the ground, cotton from a plant and wool from a sheep become pots and cloth.
A kiln's heat bakes the clay hard so it cannot go back to mud.
Potters and weavers work with their hands, and the skill passes down in families.
The weaver's cloth has a pattern of threads that repeat.
Each state has its own crafts that tell us about the people of that place.
Salt crystals form flat faces as the water dries up.
The Sun dries the water and leaves salt behind.
Rocks break slowly into soil over a very long time.
We take things from the earth, so we must use them carefully so they last.
The workers do hard jobs in the heat, and their work gives us salt and stone.
Rockets have to carry their own air and fuel, because space has none.
A plane has wings that push air down, and the air pushes the plane up.
Rockets go out to the Moon and the planets in our solar system.
Many inventions began with mistakes and trying again.
India sent its own rockets and satellites into space, and people worked hard for years to do it.

acts.name: Water park or swimming pool visit

links.why: Water on the slide makes it slippery, so you slide faster.
You feel lighter in water, because the water pushes up against you.
Water pools hold tiny things that live in them if they are not cleaned.
A shower before and after keeps the pool and our skin clean.
Always swim with a grown-up and follow the lifeguard.
A house stands up because of its strong foundation and walls.
Bricks, steel, cement and glass are each chosen for a different job.
A pulley or a crane lifts heavy loads to the top.
The builders measure every wall to make sure it is straight and the right length.
Masons, electricians and plumbers all work together on a house.
Waste is sorted into types so that each can be reused or recycled.
Kitchen waste turns into soil in the compost pit.
A banana peel rots but plastic stays for years, so we use less plastic.
The scrap dealer weighs paper, metal and plastic to give a price per kilo.
If paper fetches 12 rupees a kilo, how much for 5 kilos?
Read the menu: how much will our order cost altogether?
Try to choose a plate with grain, dal, vegetables and curd.
Clean hands and fresh food keep us from getting a tummy ache.
Order your own food, and say please and thank you.
Each state has its own food, so what is this dish and where does it come from?
Grandparents were children once, and bodies change from baby to old age.
Draw how everyone in the family is related to you.
Ask your grandparent what they played and ate when they were your age.
Ask your grandparent three questions and listen to the answers.
The language or dialect at your grandparents' home may be different from yours.
People travel to holy places to pray, and each faith has its own.
Find the holy place on the map and trace the route.
Pilgrims go by train, bus, boat or on foot, depending on where they are going.
Long walks make muscles tired, so we rest and drink water.
On the way, notice how food, dress and language change.
A ball flies in an arc because gravity pulls it down while it moves forward.
The scoreboard shows runs and wickets; we can draw a graph of the scores.
If one team has 120 and the other 98, who is ahead and by how many?
The roar of the crowd reaches you after you see the shot, because sound is slower than light.
Every game has rules, and fair play means everyone follows them.
We see when light comes into our eyes, and glasses help the eye focus it.
A lens in spectacles bends light so a clear picture forms.
The dentist checks your teeth, and brushing keeps them strong.
Washing hands and brushing teeth keep germs away.
Loud sounds can hurt our ears, so we protect our hearing.
A forest gives animals food, water and a place to hide.
Trees give fruit and shade to animals, and animals spread the seeds.
Fallen leaves are turned into soil by worms and moulds.
Look for trees, climbers, shrubs and grass and see how their stems differ.
Forests give us air, water and wood, so we must keep them safe.
